front_blocks.md: Define **ion**.

back_blocks.md: An **ion** is an electrically charged atom or group of atoms formed by the **loss** or **gain** of electrons.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Atoms form ions by gaining or losing electrons to achieve a full outer shell.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Atoms gain or lose electrons so that their outer shell becomes **full**, giving them the same electronic structure as a **noble gas**.

front_blocks.md: Define **anion**.

back_blocks.md: An **anion** is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom **gains** electrons, so it has more electrons than protons.

front_blocks.md: Why do atoms form ions rather than staying as neutral atoms?

back_blocks.md: Atoms form ions because gaining or losing electrons gives them a **full outer shell** of electrons. This is a more stable electronic arrangement, the same as that of a **noble gas**.

front_blocks.md: When a metal atom loses electrons, it forms a **..........** ion. When a non-metal atom gains electrons, it forms a **..........** ion.

back_blocks.md: When a metal atom loses electrons, it forms a **positive** ion. When a non-metal atom gains electrons, it forms a **negative** ion.

front_blocks.md: Define **cation**.

back_blocks.md: A **cation** is a positively charged ion formed when an atom **loses** electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.

front_blocks.md: How does the charge on an ion relate to the number of electrons gained or lost?

back_blocks.md: The charge on an ion equals the number of electrons gained or lost. For example, losing **2 electrons** gives a **2+ charge**, and gaining **1 electron** gives a **1– charge**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All non-metals lose electrons to form negatively charged ions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
All non-metals **gain** electrons from other atoms to become negatively charged **anions**. It is metals that lose electrons.

front_blocks.md: How do you work out the charge on an ion from its position in the periodic table?

back_blocks.md: How you work out the charge depends on whether the atom gains or loses electrons. Atoms with **fewer than 4 outer electrons** tend to lose them and form **positive ions**, while atoms with **more than 4** tend to gain electrons and form **negative ions**.

front_blocks.md: What are **compound ions**?

front_blocks.md: What is the **swap-and-drop method**?

back_blocks.md: The **swap-and-drop method** is a technique for finding the formula of an ionic compound: the size of the charge on each ion becomes the subscript number for the other ion, giving the correct ratio.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds have no overall charge?

back_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have no overall charge because the **positive charges** from the metal ions are exactly **cancelled out** by the negative charges from the non-metal ions. The total charge across the compound equals zero.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
CuCl is the correct formula for copper(II) chloride.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Copper(II) has a 2+ charge and chloride has a 1– charge. Using the swap-and-drop method, two chloride ions are needed to cancel the 2+ charge, so the correct formula is CuCl<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: How do you use the direct comparison method to find the formula of an ionic compound?

back_blocks.md: Write down the charges of both ions and check whether they cancel each other out. If the charges are **equal and opposite**, one of each ion is needed. If they are not equal, adjust the number of each ion until the **total charge is zero**.

front_blocks.md: What is a **giant ionic lattice**?

back_blocks.md: A **giant ionic lattice** is a regular three-dimensional arrangement of thousands of alternating positive and negative ions held together by strong **electrostatic forces of attraction** acting in all directions.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points?

back_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points because they contain a **giant ionic lattice** with **strong electrostatic forces of attraction** between oppositely charged ions acting in all directions. A large amount of **energy** is needed to overcome these forces.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds can conduct electricity in the solid state.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In the solid state, ions are held in **fixed positions** in the lattice and cannot move. Because the ions cannot move, they cannot carry a charge and the compound cannot conduct electricity.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when they are melted or dissolved in water?

back_blocks.md: When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water, the **ions are free to move**. These moving ions can carry a charge through the liquid, allowing electricity to flow.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride because its ions have a greater charge.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

Magnesium oxide contains Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> ions, which have a **greater charge** than the Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions in sodium chloride. Greater ionic charges mean stronger **electrostatic forces**, requiring more energy to overcome.

back_blocks.md: **Electrostatic forces of attraction** are the strong forces between oppositely charged **positive** and **negative** ions in an ionic compound. They act in all directions and hold the giant ionic lattice together.

back_blocks.md: The greater the charge on the ions, the **stronger the electrostatic forces** between them. Stronger forces require more **energy** to overcome, so the melting point is **higher**.
